title: My Mother at Sixty-Six
summary: Driving to the Cochin airport, Kamala Das notices how old and pale her sixty-six-year-old mother looks as she dozes beside her, and is struck by the fear of losing her. She turns to the lively world outside, but at the airport the same fear returns; she hides her pain behind a smile and a casual promise to see her soon.

notes.heading: About the poet
notes.html: Kamala Das (1934–2009) was an Indian poet writing in English and Malayalam (as Madhavikutty). Her confessional poetry deals frankly with love, loneliness and the self.

notes.heading: Gist
notes.html: The poem captures a single moment of emotional realisation. As the poet drives with her mother, she sees the old woman’s face, slack and colourless in sleep, and feels a pang at the thought of her approaching death. She distracts herself by watching young trees and playful children outside. At the airport security check, she looks at her mother again and feels the old childhood fear, but bids her goodbye with a smile.

notes.heading: Stanza-wise explanation (paraphrase)
notes.html:
The poem is a single stanza of 14 lines, but can be read in four movements.

Lines 1–6: The realisation. Last Friday morning the poet is driving from her parents’ home to Cochin airport. Her mother sits beside her, dozing with her mouth open. Her face looks ashen, like that of a dead person. With pain, the poet realises that her mother has grown very old.

Lines 6–9: Escape to the outside. To push the painful thought away, she looks out of the car window. She sees young trees that seem to be running past and children joyfully rushing out of their homes. These images of youth and energy contrast with her mother’s age.

Lines 9–12: The airport. After the security check, standing a few yards away, she looks at her mother again. Her mother’s face appears wan and pale, like the faint moon of late winter. The poet feels the familiar ache of her childhood fear of losing her mother.

Lines 12–14: The farewell. She does not express her feelings. Instead she says she will see her soon and keeps smiling, repeating the smile as if to reassure herself and her mother.

notes.heading: Poetic devices
notes.html:
• Simile: the mother’s face is compared to a corpse’s and to the late winter moon.
  • Personification / transferred motion: trees are pictured as sprinting past the car.
  • Contrast: the ageing mother versus young trees and merry children; inner sorrow versus outward smile.
  • Imagery: visual images of the ashen face, the running trees and pale moon.
  • Repetition: the repeated ‘smile’ at the end stresses the effort to hide emotion.
  • Free verse and enjambment: no regular rhyme; lines run on like a flow of thought.
  • Single sentence form: the poem flows like one continuous emotional experience.

notes.heading: Themes
notes.html:
• Ageing and mortality: the inevitability of old age and death.
  • Fear of separation: a child’s lifelong fear of losing a parent.
  • Love and helplessness: deep love that cannot stop time.
  • Concealing emotion: adults hide sorrow behind smiles.

notes.heading: Title justification
notes.html: The title directly points to the subject, the poet’s mother at the age of sixty-six, an age when signs of decline become visible. It sets the focus on ageing and on the poet’s emotional response to it.

notes.heading: Message and values
notes.html: Life is transient, and our parents will not be with us forever. We should value and care for them while they are with us, and accept ageing as a natural part of life.

keyTerms.definition: Very pale, the colour of ash; describes the mother’s sleeping face.
A dead body; the poet compares her mother’s face to one, expressing fear of death.
A comparison using ‘like’ or ‘as’, e.g. the face compared to the late winter moon.
Giving human qualities to non-human things, e.g. trees sprinting.
Placing opposite images side by side: the old mother and the lively children.
Poetry that openly expresses the poet’s personal emotions and experiences.
Continuation of a sentence beyond the end of a line without a pause.

mcqs.q: Where was the poet driving to?
mcqs.explanation: She was driving from her parents’ home to Cochin airport.

mcqs.q: Why does the poet compare her mother’s face to that of a corpse?
options: Her mother was sleeping with a pale, lifeless look, suggesting old age and nearing death.
mcqs.explanation: The ashen, slack face of the sleeping old woman reminded the poet of death.

mcqs.q: Why did the poet look out of the window?
options: To distract herself from the painful thought of her mother’s ageing
mcqs.explanation: She turned to the outside world to push away the painful thought.

mcqs.q: The young trees ‘sprinting’ is an example of:
mcqs.explanation: Trees cannot run; giving them a human action is personification.

mcqs.q: What do the merry children symbolise?
mcqs.explanation: They represent youth and vitality, in contrast to the ageing mother.

mcqs.q: To what does the poet compare her mother’s face at the airport?
mcqs.explanation: Pale and faded, her face looks like the late winter’s moon.

mcqs.q: What was the poet’s childhood fear?
mcqs.explanation: The old ache is the fear of losing her mother, felt since childhood.

mcqs.q: Why does the poet keep smiling at the end?
options: To hide her pain and reassure her mother
She is excited about the flight.
mcqs.explanation: The smile masks her fear and sorrow and comforts her mother.

mcqs.q: Which feature describes the structure of the poem?
options: A sonnet with rhyme scheme ABAB
A single stanza in free verse written as one long sentence
mcqs.explanation: The poem is one stanza in free verse, flowing as a single sentence.

mcqs.q: The dominant mood of the poem is:
mcqs.explanation: The poem is poignant, tinged with sadness and fear of loss.

questions.q:
Read the situation and answer: Standing a few yards away after the security check, the poet looks back at her mother and finds her face pale and faded, like a moon in the last days of winter.
(a) What feeling returns to the poet at this moment? (1)
(b) Identify the figure of speech. (1)
(c) Why is the image of late winter apt? (1)
(d) How does the poet respond outwardly? (1)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) Her childhood fear of losing her mother.

(b) Simile.

(c) Late winter suggests the end of a season, just as her mother is in the last phase of life; the moon is pale and lifeless.

(d) She smiles and says she will see her soon.

questions.q: What is the significance of the young trees and merry children in the poem?
questions.answerHtml: They represent youth, energy and life, in contrast to the ageing, pale mother. By looking at them, the poet tries to distract herself from the painful thought of her mother’s decline. The contrast heightens the sense of age and mortality.

questions.q: Why does the poet compare her mother to a corpse?
questions.answerHtml: As her mother dozes with her mouth open, her face looks pale, ashen and lifeless. This makes the poet suddenly aware of her old age and the nearness of death, and the comparison expresses her deep fear of losing her.

questions.q: What do the parting words and the smile of the poet suggest?
questions.answerHtml: They suggest that the poet hides her sorrow and fear to avoid upsetting her mother. Saying she will see her soon is a hopeful assurance, while the repeated smile reveals the effort it takes to stay composed at an emotional moment.

questions.q: Discuss how Kamala Das uses contrast and imagery to convey her feelings in ‘My Mother at Sixty-Six’. (120–150 words)
questions.answerHtml:
Kamala Das builds the poem on striking contrasts and vivid images. Inside the car, her mother dozes with an ashen, corpse-like face, an image that signals old age and death. Outside, young trees seem to sprint past and children rush merrily out of their homes. The contrast between the stillness of age and the movement of youth sharpens the poet’s pain.

At the airport another image appears: her mother’s face, pale and wan like the moon of late winter, suggesting the fading of life at the end of a season. This brings back her childhood fear of losing her mother.

The final contrast is between inner feeling and outward behaviour. Though anguished, the poet says only that she will see her soon and keeps smiling. Through these contrasts and images, the poet conveys her love, helplessness and the universal fear of separation from a parent.

questions.q: ‘My Mother at Sixty-Six’ is a poem about the universal fear of ageing and separation. Explain. (120–150 words)
questions.answerHtml:
Although the poem describes a single drive to the airport, the feelings it captures are universal. Every child, at some point, suddenly notices that a parent has grown old. The poet experiences this when she sees her sixty-six-year-old mother dozing, her face pale and lifeless like a corpse.

The realisation awakens the deepest fear of a child, the fear of losing one’s mother. The poet tries to escape it by looking at the youthful world outside, but at the security check the fear returns. Her mother’s face now looks like the pale late-winter moon, reminding her that life is passing.

Like most people, she cannot speak of her feelings. She hides them behind a smile and a casual promise to meet again. The poem thus reflects the common human experience of loving, fearing loss, and accepting the inevitability of ageing and death with quiet courage.
